claim: The entorhinal cortex (EC) defines the interface between the hippocampus and the neocortex.
source: The entorhinal cortex (EC)—defining the interface between the hippocampus and the neocortex (Munoz and Insausti, 2005)—plays a pivotal role in the integration of different sensory inputs into higher order mnemonic representations (Eichenbaum et al., 2007; Moser and Moser, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Munoz and Insausti, 2005.

claim: The entorhinal cortex plays a pivotal role in the integration of different sensory inputs into higher order mnemonic representations.
source: The entorhinal cortex (EC)—defining the interface between the hippocampus and the neocortex (Munoz and Insausti, 2005)—plays a pivotal role in the integration of different sensory inputs into higher order mnemonic representations (Eichenbaum et al., 2007; Moser and Moser, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Eichenbaum et al., 2007 and Moser and Moser, 2013.

claim: In rodents, the EC is typically subdivided into two major subregions, the medial- and the lateral entorhinal cortex (MEC and LEC, respectively), based on cytoarchitectonics.
source: In rodents—and on the basis of cytoarchitectonics—the EC is typically (Kerr et al., 2007; Canto et al., 2008; Van Strien et al., 2009) subdivided into two major subregions, the medial- and the lateral entorhinal cortex (MEC and LEC, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kerr et al., 2007; Canto et al., 2008; Van Strien et al., 2009.

claim: The MEC receives inputs about spatial information from parahippocampal cortex (PHC).
source: The MEC receives inputs about spatial information from parahippocampal cortex (PHC) and the LEC receives item-related information from perirhinal cortex (PRC) (Van Strien et al., 2009; Deshmukh and Knierim, 2011; Ranganath and Ritchey, 2012; Knierim et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Van Strien et al., 2009; Deshmukh and Knierim, 2011; Ranganath and Ritchey, 2012; Knierim et al., 2013.

claim: The LEC receives item-related information from perirhinal cortex (PRC).
source: The MEC receives inputs about spatial information from parahippocampal cortex (PHC) and the LEC receives item-related information from perirhinal cortex (PRC) (Van Strien et al., 2009; Deshmukh and Knierim, 2011; Ranganath and Ritchey, 2012; Knierim et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Van Strien et al., 2009; Deshmukh and Knierim, 2011; Ranganath and Ritchey, 2012; Knierim et al., 2013.

claim: Similar functional roles of the PHC and PRC have been described in humans.
source: Similar functional roles of the PHC and PRC have been described in humans (Epstein and Kanwisher, 1998; Davachi et al., 2003; Eichenbaum et al., 2007; Ekstrom and Bookheimer, 2007; Litman et al., 2009; Duarte et al., 2011; Staresina et al., 2011; Martin et al., 2013; Vilberg and Davachi, 2013) and relate to distinct visual processing streams (Kravitz et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to human studies.

claim: The functional roles of PHC and PRC relate to distinct visual processing streams.
source: Similar functional roles of the PHC and PRC have been described in humans (Epstein and Kanwisher, 1998; Davachi et al., 2003; Eichenbaum et al., 2007; Ekstrom and Bookheimer, 2007; Litman et al., 2009; Duarte et al., 2011; Staresina et al., 2011; Martin et al., 2013; Vilberg and Davachi, 2013) and relate to distinct visual processing streams (Kravitz et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kravitz et al., 2011.

claim: The MEC contains a high proportion of head-direction and grid cells.
source: The MEC contains a high proportion of head-direction and grid cells, whose activity is modulated by running direction and spatial location, respectively (Hafting et al., 2005; Sargolini et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hafting et al., 2005 and Sargolini et al., 2006.

claim: Grid cell activity is modulated by spatial location.
source: The MEC contains a high proportion of head-direction and grid cells, whose activity is modulated by running direction and spatial location, respectively (Hafting et al., 2005; Sargolini et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hafting et al., 2005 and Sargolini et al., 2006.

claim: Head-direction cell activity is modulated by running direction.
source: The MEC contains a high proportion of head-direction and grid cells, whose activity is modulated by running direction and spatial location, respectively (Hafting et al., 2005; Sargolini et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hafting et al., 2005 and Sargolini et al., 2006.

claim: Cells in the LEC respond to individual objects in the environment rather than to specific locations.
source: In contrast, cells in the LEC respond to individual objects in the environment rather than to specific locations (Deshmukh and Knierim, 2011; Tsao et al., 2013; Knierim et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Deshmukh and Knierim, 2011; Tsao et al., 2013; Knierim et al., 2013.

claim: AD pathology starts in the EC.
source: This hampers translational studies, which is particularly relevant in the case of Alzheimer's disease (AD) with AD pathology starting in the EC (Braak and Braak, 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Braak and Braak, 1992.

claim: Within the EC, the vulnerability to AD-related pathology is not homogeneously distributed and differs between medial and lateral strips in humans.
source: Within the EC, the vulnerability to AD-related pathology is not homogeneously distributed and differs between medial and lateral strips in humans, which has been related to similar findings in the rodent MEC and LEC, respectively (Khan et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Khan et al., 2014.

claim: The MEC is located medially in the septal (posterior) part of the EC in rodents.
source: Rather, the MEC is located medially in the septal (posterior) part of the EC and the LEC is located laterally in the temporal (anterior) part of the EC in rodents (Van Strien et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Van Strien et al., 2009.

claim: The LEC is located laterally in the temporal (anterior) part of the EC in rodents.
source: Rather, the MEC is located medially in the septal (posterior) part of the EC and the LEC is located laterally in the temporal (anterior) part of the EC in rodents (Van Strien et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Van Strien et al., 2009.

claim: Tracing studies on PHC and PRC pathways in non-human primates suggest a dominant anterior-posterior division.
source: Furthermore, tracing studies on PHC and PRC pathways in non-human primates suggest a dominant anterior-posterior division (Suzuki and Amaral, 1994; Insausti and Amaral, 2008), as do single-unit recordings that show activity consistent with the rodent LEC in the anterior EC in primates (Killian et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Suzuki and Amaral, 1994 and Insausti and Amaral, 2008.

claim: Single-unit recordings show activity consistent with the rodent LEC in the anterior EC in primates.
source: Furthermore, tracing studies on PHC and PRC pathways in non-human primates suggest a dominant anterior-posterior division (Suzuki and Amaral, 1994; Insausti and Amaral, 2008), as do single-unit recordings that show activity consistent with the rodent LEC in the anterior EC in primates (Killian et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Killian et al., 2012.

claim: Neuroimaging studies on memory in healthy participants suggest that the rodent MEC and LEC map on medial and lateral strips of EC in humans.
source: In contrast, neuroimaging studies on memory in healthy participants (Schultz et al., 2012; Reagh and Yassa, 2014) and participants with preclinical AD (Khan et al., 2014) suggest that the rodent MEC and LEC map on medial and lateral strips of EC in humans.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Schultz et al., 2012 and Reagh and Yassa, 2014.

claim: The EC is 25–30 mm2 in humans.
source: To resolve this discrepancy in the literature, one needs to investigate the relatively small EC (25–30 mm2 in humans) (Krimer et al., 1997) with high anatomical precision.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Krimer et al., 1997.

claim: MEC and LEC exhibit differential connectivity with cortical regions.
source: Specifically, it has been shown that MEC and LEC exhibit differential connectivity with cortical regions (Witter and Groenewegen, 1989; Kerr et al., 2007; Van Strien et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Witter and Groenewegen, 1989; Kerr et al., 2007; Van Strien et al., 2009.

claim: Differential fingerprints of anatomical connectivity should lead to differences in functional connectivity identifiable with fMRI.
source: The differential fingerprints of anatomical connectivity should lead to differences in functional connectivity identifiable with fMRI (Johansen-Berg et al., 2004; Buckner et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Johansen-Berg et al., 2004; Buckner et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2014.

claim: A recent model on cortical memory networks posits that an anterior-temporal (AT) system converges on the PRC and a posterior-medial (PM) system on the PHC.
source: A recent model on cortical memory networks (Ranganath and Ritchey, 2012) posits that an anterior-temporal (AT) system converges on the PRC and a posterior-medial (PM) system on the PHC.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ranganath and Ritchey, 2012.

claim: Based on studies in rodents, the two networks are hypothesised to connect to either the LEC or the MEC, respectively.
source: Based on studies in rodents, the two networks are hypothesised to connect to either the LEC or the MEC, respectively (Witter and Groenewegen, 1989; Kerr et al., 2007; Van Strien et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Witter and Groenewegen, 1989; Kerr et al., 2007; Van Strien et al., 2009.

claim: Studies in non-human primates predict that the entorhinal projections of the two systems show a strong anteroposterior division.
source: Studies in non-human primates predict that the entorhinal projections of the two systems show a strong anteroposterior division (Suzuki and Amaral, 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Suzuki and Amaral, 1994.

claim: There was a main effect of network on entorhinal connectivity (repeated-measures ANOVA: F(1,21) = 10.0, p = 0.005).
source: We found a main effect of network on entorhinal connectivity (repeated-measures ANOVA: F(1,21) = 10.0, p = 0.005).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from the navigation experiment.

claim: The lateral parts of EC connected stronger to the AT compared to the PM network (T(21) = 2.6, p = 0.015).
source: Post-hoc t-tests revealed that the lateral parts of EC connected stronger to the AT compared to the PM network (T(21) = 2.6, p = 0.015; medial parts of EC: T(21) = −0.2 p = 0.83).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from the navigation experiment.

claim: Medial parts of EC did not show differential connectivity between AT and PM networks (T(21) = −0.2 p = 0.83).
source: Post-hoc t-tests revealed that the lateral parts of EC connected stronger to the AT compared to the PM network (T(21) = 2.6, p = 0.015; medial parts of EC: T(21) = −0.2 p = 0.83).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from the navigation experiment.

claim: There was a connectivity difference along the anteroposterior axis (repeated-measures ANOVA: main effect of network, F(1,21) = 13.2, p = 0.001).
source: However, in contrast to previous suggestions, we additionally observed a connectivity difference along the anteroposterior axis (repeated-measures ANOVA: main effect of network, F(1,21) = 13.2, p = 0.001) and post-hoc t-tests showed that the anterior parts of EC connected more with the AT compared to the PM network (T(21) = 2.7: p = 0.01; posterior EC: T(21) = −0.49, p = 0.63).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from the navigation experiment.

claim: The anterior parts of EC connected more with the AT compared to the PM network (T(21) = 2.7: p = 0.01).
source: However, in contrast to previous suggestions, we additionally observed a connectivity difference along the anteroposterior axis (repeated-measures ANOVA: main effect of network, F(1,21) = 13.2, p = 0.001) and post-hoc t-tests showed that the anterior parts of EC connected more with the AT compared to the PM network (T(21) = 2.7: p = 0.01; posterior EC: T(21) = −0.49, p = 0.63).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from the navigation experiment.

claim: Posterior EC did not show differential connectivity between AT and PM networks (T(21) = −0.49, p = 0.63).
source: However, in contrast to previous suggestions, we additionally observed a connectivity difference along the anteroposterior axis (repeated-measures ANOVA: main effect of network, F(1,21) = 13.2, p = 0.001) and post-hoc t-tests showed that the anterior parts of EC connected more with the AT compared to the PM network (T(21) = 2.7: p = 0.01; posterior EC: T(21) = −0.49, p = 0.63).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from the navigation experiment.

claim: The dominant mode of functional connectivity change extended along the long-axis of the EC, approximately from the posterior to the anterior end.
source: Applied to the fMRI data acquired while subjects performed the virtual-reality task, we observed that the dominant mode of functional connectivity change extended along the long-axis of the EC, approximately from the posterior to the anterior end (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), while the orientation of the second was largely perpendicular (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data-driven connectivity analysis results shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The orientation of the second-dominant mode of connectivity change was largely perpendicular to the first.
source: Applied to the fMRI data acquired while subjects performed the virtual-reality task, we observed that the dominant mode of functional connectivity change extended along the long-axis of the EC, approximately from the posterior to the anterior end (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), while the orientation of the second was largely perpendicular (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data-driven connectivity analysis results shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both modes of connectivity change could be reliably detected using an independent resting-state fMRI dataset.
source: Both modes of connectivity change could also be reliably detected using an independent resting-state fMRI dataset (60 subjects of the WU-Minn Human Connectome Project; see 'Materials and methods'), suggesting that the organization of EC functional connectivity is largely task-independent (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of independent resting-state data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The organization of EC functional connectivity is largely task-independent.
source: Both modes of connectivity change could also be reliably detected using an independent resting-state fMRI dataset (60 subjects of the WU-Minn Human Connectome Project; see 'Materials and methods'), suggesting that the organization of EC functional connectivity is largely task-independent (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the reproducibility of connectivity patterns across task and resting-state data.

claim: The first dominant mode of functional connectivity change was highly reproducible across resting-state sessions (Pearson's R = 0.99, p < 0.001).
source: Both the first and second-dominant modes of functional connectivity change were highly reproducible across resting-state sessions (Pearson's R = 0.99, p < 0.001 and Pearson's R = 0.98, p < 0.001, for the dominant and second-dominant modes, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of resting-state data reproducibility.

claim: The second-dominant mode of functional connectivity change was highly reproducible across resting-state sessions (Pearson's R = 0.98, p < 0.001).
source: Both the first and second-dominant modes of functional connectivity change were highly reproducible across resting-state sessions (Pearson's R = 0.99, p < 0.001 and Pearson's R = 0.98, p < 0.001, for the dominant and second-dominant modes, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of resting-state data reproducibility.

claim: One division contained the posterior EC and the other division included most of the anterior EC.
source: 3D-rendering of the two clusters derived from the dominant mode of connectivity change revealed a consistent topology across hemispheres (Figure 2B, Video 1). One division contained the posterior EC (Figure 2—figure supplement 1—displayed in blue). The other division included most of the anterior EC (Figure 2—figure supplement 1—displayed in red).
evidence: The claim is supported by 3D rendering and visualization shown in Figure 2B, Video 1, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The posterior cluster was located more medially (and to some extent more dorsally) and the anterior cluster was located more laterally (and to some extent more ventrally).
source: In addition to the dominant anterior-posterior distinction, the posterior cluster was located more medially (and to some extent more dorsally) and the anterior cluster was located more laterally (and to some extent more ventrally).
evidence: The claim is supported by spatial analysis of cluster locations from the data-driven connectivity analysis.

claim: Group-level contrasts showed peaks in the medial-prefrontal and orbitofrontal cortex for the alEC.
source: Group-level contrasts showed peaks in the medial-prefrontal and orbitofrontal cortex for the alEC, regions associated with the AT system.
evidence: The claim is supported by whole-volume connectivity analysis results.

claim: Occipital and posterior-parietal cortex was dominated by connectivity with the pmEC.
source: In contrast, occipital and posterior-parietal cortex was dominated by connectivity with the pmEC, areas associated with the PM system (Ranganath and Ritchey, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by whole-volume connectivity analysis results.

claim: The pmEC showed increased connectivity with frontal regions.
source: In addition, the pmEC showed increased connectivity with frontal regions (see Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by connectivity analysis results shown in Figure 2D.

claim: These findings are in line with the patterns of reciprocal connections of the rodent LEC and MEC, respectively.
source: These findings are in line with the patterns of reciprocal connections of the rodent LEC and MEC, respectively (Kerr et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with known rodent connectivity patterns cited from Kerr et al., 2007.

claim: tSNR did not differ between alEC and pmEC (T(21) = 0.2, p = 0.83).
source: Furthermore, we examined both spatial and temporal SNR (tSNR) of the alEC and the pmEC (Figure 2—figure supplement 3). tSNR did not differ between alEC and pmEC (T(21) = 0.2, p = 0.83) but spatial SNR did (T(21) = 9.7, p < 0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of SNR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Spatial SNR differed between alEC and pmEC (T(21) = 9.7, p < 0.001).
source: Furthermore, we examined both spatial and temporal SNR (tSNR) of the alEC and the pmEC (Figure 2—figure supplement 3). tSNR did not differ between alEC and pmEC (T(21) = 0.2, p = 0.83) but spatial SNR did (T(21) = 9.7, p < 0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of SNR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Signal was higher in the pmEC compared to the alEC (mean signal: alEC = 4.97; mean signal pmEC = 7.76; T(21) = 38, p < 0.001).
source: This was associated with higher signal in the pmEC compared to the alEC (mean signal: alEC = 4.97; mean signal pmEC = 7.76; T(21) = 38, p < 0.001) in the absence of differences in spatial standard deviation (T(21) = 1.5, p = 0.144).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of signal intensity data.

claim: There were no differences in spatial standard deviation between alEC and pmEC (T(21) = 1.5, p = 0.144).
source: This was associated with higher signal in the pmEC compared to the alEC (mean signal: alEC = 4.97; mean signal pmEC = 7.76; T(21) = 38, p < 0.001) in the absence of differences in spatial standard deviation (T(21) = 1.5, p = 0.144).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of signal variability data.

claim: Mean signal was subtracted from time-series prior to all connectivity analyses, which makes it unlikely that signal intensity differences affected the connectivity results.
source: Note, that mean signal was subtracted from time-series prior to all connectivity analyses (see 'Materials and methods'), which makes it unlikely that signal intensity differences affected the connectivity results.
evidence: The claim is based on the preprocessing procedure described in the methods.

claim: Motion scrubbing had only minimal effects on the results.
source: However, we additionally repeated the data-driven connectivity analysis after excluding time periods with large head movements (motion scrubbing [Power et al., 2012, 2015]). Motion scrubbing had only minimal effects on the results.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of results before and after motion scrubbing.

claim: Pearson correlation coefficients of the pre- and post scrubbing results were close to 1 and highly significant (gradient one: left R = 0.9964, right R = 0.9958; gradient two: left = 0.9348, right = 0.8816; all p values <0.001).
source: Pearson correlation coefficients of the pre- and post scrubbing results were close to 1 and highly significant (gradient one: left R = 0.9964, right R = 0.9958; gradient two: left = 0.9348, right = 0.8816; all p values <0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison of results before and after motion scrubbing.

claim: Homologous connectivity exceeded non-homologous connectivity (T(21) = 4.05, p = 0.0006).
source: Here we observed that homologous connectivity indeed exceeded non-homologous connectivity (Figure 2—figure supplement 4). Importantly, this was also the case if non-homologous connectivity was assessed within the same hemisphere, between adjacent parts of the EC (T(21) = 4.05, p = 0.0006).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of connectivity patterns shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Higher responses to spatial than non-spatial stimuli were observed in the posterior EC.
source: Here, we observed higher responses to spatial than non-spatial stimuli in the posterior EC, while the inverse contrast (objects vs scenes) showed higher responses in the anterior EC (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by univariate fMRI analysis results shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The inverse contrast (objects vs scenes) showed higher responses in the anterior EC.
source: Here, we observed higher responses to spatial than non-spatial stimuli in the posterior EC, while the inverse contrast (objects vs scenes) showed higher responses in the anterior EC (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by univariate fMRI analysis results shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The anterior-lateral cluster showed higher sensitivity to non-spatial stimuli compared to the PM cluster (T(20) = 4.9, p = 0.0001).
source: ROI analyses using the clusters derived from the dominant mode of connectivity change revealed that the anterior-lateral cluster showed higher sensitivity to non-spatial stimuli compared to the PM cluster (T(20) = 4.9, p = 0.0001, Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by ROI analysis results shown in Figure 2C.

claim: This dissociation was not present for the clusters that were derived from the second-dominant mode of connectivity change within the EC (T(20) = −0.26, p = 0.8).
source: This dissociation was not present for the clusters that were derived from the second-dominant mode of connectivity change within the EC (T(20) = −0.26, p = 0.8; Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by ROI analysis results shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The human homologue of the rodent MEC maps predominantly on the human posterior parts of the EC.
source: In sum, our results suggest that the human homologue of the rodent MEC maps predominantly on the human posterior parts of the EC, while the homologue of the rodent LEC maps predominantly on the anterior parts of the EC.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results of connectivity and functional sensitivity analyses.

claim: The homologue of the rodent LEC maps predominantly on the anterior parts of the EC.
source: In sum, our results suggest that the human homologue of the rodent MEC maps predominantly on the human posterior parts of the EC, while the homologue of the rodent LEC maps predominantly on the anterior parts of the EC.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results of connectivity and functional sensitivity analyses.

claim: The EC, in concert with the hippocampus, plays a crucial role in memory and learning.
source: The EC, in concert with the hippocampus, plays a crucial role in memory and learning (Eichenbaum et al., 2007) and is the core of the brain's navigational system (Moser and Moser, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Eichenbaum et al., 2007.

claim: The EC is the core of the brain's navigational system.
source: The EC, in concert with the hippocampus, plays a crucial role in memory and learning (Eichenbaum et al., 2007) and is the core of the brain's navigational system (Moser and Moser, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Moser and Moser, 2013.

claim: The anatomical organisation and connectivity patterns of the EC are largely conserved across species.
source: While the shape and location of the EC differs between rodents and primates (Witter and Groenewegen, 1989), the anatomical organisation and connectivity patterns are largely conserved across species (Canto et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Witter and Groenewegen, 1989 and Canto et al., 2008.

claim: The shape and location of the EC differs between rodents and primates.
source: While the shape and location of the EC differs between rodents and primates (Witter and Groenewegen, 1989), the anatomical organisation and connectivity patterns are largely conserved across species (Canto et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Witter and Groenewegen, 1989.

claim: It is unlikely that medial and lateral strips of EC in humans correspond to the rodent MEC and LEC, respectively.
source: However, the anatomical locations of these cytoarchitectonically defined regions in rodents differ along more than only the mediolateral axis. More specifically, the LEC is situated more anterior-ventrally, whereas the MEC is situated more posterior-dorsally in rodents (Van Strien et al., 2009). Therefore, it is unlikely that medial and lateral strips of EC in humans correspond to the rodent MEC and LEC, respectively.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the anatomical differences between rodent and human EC organization.

claim: In primates the characteristic projections from the PRC and PHC strongly map onto the anteroposterior axis.
source: Furthermore, in primates the characteristic projections from the PRC and PHC strongly map onto the anteroposterior axis (Suzuki and Amaral, 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Suzuki and Amaral, 1994.

claim: Both model-based and data-driven connectivity analyses, as well as sensitivity to non-spatial vs spatial stimuli provide evidence for an anterior-lateral and a PM localisation of the homologues of the rodent LEC and MEC, respectively.
source: Here, we leveraged the distinct connectivity fingerprints and functional roles (such as complementary computation of scene and object information) of the rodent LEC and MEC to find their human homologues with fMRI with three complementary methods and three independent datasets. Both model-based and data-driven connectivity analyses, as well as sensitivity to non-spatial vs spatial stimuli provide evidence for an anterior-lateral and a PM localisation of the homologues of the rodent LEC and MEC, respectively.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main findings from multiple analyses across three datasets.

claim: Maass et al confirmed these findings in a study with two high-resolution, high-field fMRI datasets by focusing on local connectivity between regions of the medial temporal lobes.
source: Maass et al confirmed these findings in a study with two high-resolution, high-field fMRI datasets by focusing on local connectivity between regions of the medial temporal lobes.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Maass et al., 2015.

claim: Maass et al found preferential connectivity of PRC and proximal subiculum to anterior-lateral parts of the EC.
source: They found preferential connectivity of PRC and proximal subiculum to anterior-lateral parts of the EC, whereas posterior-medial parts of the EC were more connected to PHC and distal subiculum.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to findings from Maass et al., 2015.

claim: Posterior-medial parts of the EC were more connected to PHC and distal subiculum.
source: They found preferential connectivity of PRC and proximal subiculum to anterior-lateral parts of the EC, whereas posterior-medial parts of the EC were more connected to PHC and distal subiculum.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to findings from Maass et al., 2015.

claim: The data-driven connectivity analysis revealed a second organisation structure approximately perpendicular to the first.
source: In addition to the change in functional connectivity from PM to anterior-lateral, our data-driven connectivity analysis also revealed a second organisation structure approximately perpendicular to the first (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), which might reflect bands of intra-entorhinal projections that are known to cross the LEC/MEC boundary in a roughly orthogonal orientation in rodents (Canto et al., 2008) and in primates (Chrobak and Amaral, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by data-driven connectivity analysis results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The second organisation structure might reflect bands of intra-entorhinal projections that are known to cross the LEC/MEC boundary in a roughly orthogonal orientation in rodents and in primates.
source: In addition to the change in functional connectivity from PM to anterior-lateral, our data-driven connectivity analysis also revealed a second organisation structure approximately perpendicular to the first (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), which might reflect bands of intra-entorhinal projections that are known to cross the LEC/MEC boundary in a roughly orthogonal orientation in rodents (Canto et al., 2008) and in primates (Chrobak and Amaral, 2007).
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on comparison with known anatomical projections cited from Canto et al., 2008 and Chrobak and Amaral, 2007.

claim: The present findings confirm three out of four complementary criteria for the definition of cortical areas: topographic organization, connectivity and functional properties.
source: Notably, the present findings confirm three out of four complementary criteria for the definition of cortical areas that have traditionally been advocated (Van Essen, 1985), namely topographic organization, connectivity and functional properties (the fourth one being cyto- and myeloarchitectonic organization).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with established criteria for cortical area definition cited from Van Essen, 1985.

claim: Previous neuroimaging studies in humans reported differences between medial and lateral aspects of EC that mimicked differences between the rodent MEC and LEC.
source: Previous neuroimaging studies in humans reported differences between medial and lateral aspects of EC that mimicked differences between the rodent MEC and LEC and assumed that both subregions are present on coronal slices of the EC (Schultz et al., 2012; Khan et al., 2014; Reagh and Yassa, 2014), that is, that the MEC and LEC correspond to medial and lateral strips of the EC.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Schultz et al., 2012; Khan et al., 2014; Reagh and Yassa, 2014.

claim: These reports could be explained by a partial overlap of the medial and lateral divisions with the pmEC and the alEC, respectively.
source: In light of our findings, these reports could be explained by a partial overlap of the medial and lateral divisions with the pmEC and the alEC, respectively.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the current findings to explain previous results.

claim: Coronal slices through the most posterior EC exclusively harbour the human homologue of the rodent MEC.
source: However, our results suggest that coronal slices through the most posterior EC exclusively harbour the human homologue of the rodent MEC.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the spatial distribution of the pmEC cluster.

claim: Anterior slices appear to contain mostly the homologue of the rodent LEC.
source: Similarly, anterior slices appear to contain mostly the homologue of the rodent LEC.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the spatial distribution of the alEC cluster.

claim: Improved mapping of homologous regions between rodents and humans should lead to increased effect sizes and more accurate interpretations.
source: Hence, improved mapping of homologous regions between rodents and humans should lead to increased effect sizes and more accurate interpretations.
evidence: The claim is a speculative prediction based on the current findings.

claim: 26 participants took part in the navigation experiment study.
source: 26 participants took part in the study (11 females, age 19–36, mean 23 years).
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about the study design.

claim: 22 participants entered the analysis and 4 were excluded due to excessive movement.
source: 22 entered the analysis and 4 were excluded due to excessive movement (number of instantaneous movements [Power et al., 2012] > 0.5 mm exceeded the mean plus 1 standard deviation).
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about the study design and data quality control.

claim: The resting-state dataset consisted of the first 60 participants of the WU-Minn Human Connectome Project (HCP).
source: The resting-state dataset consisted of the first 60 participants (41 females, age ranges: 4 between 22 and 25 years, 23 between 26 and 30 years and 33 between 31 and 35 years) of the WU-Minn Human Connectome Project (HCP) (Van Essen et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about the dataset used.

claim: 21 participants participated in the spatial and non-spatial stimulation experiment.
source: 21 participants (13 females, age 20–54, mean age 26 years) participated in the experiment.
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about the study design.

claim: Blood-oxygenation-level-dependent T2*-weighted functional images were acquired on a 7 T Siemens MAGNETOM scanner using a three dimensional echo-planar imaging (3D EPI) pulse sequence.
source: Blood-oxygenation-level-dependent T2*-weighted functional images were acquired on a 7 T Siemens MAGNETOM scanner (Siemens Healthcare, Erlangen, Germany) using a three dimensional echo-planar imaging (3D EPI) pulse sequence (Poser et al., 2010) on a 32-channel surface coil: TR = 2.7 s, TE = 20 ms, flip angle = 14°, slice thickness = 0.92 mm, slice oversampling = 8.3%, in-plane resolution = 0.9^2 mm, field of view (FoV) = 210 mm in each direction, 96 slices, phase encoding acceleration factor = 4, 3D acceleration factor = 2.
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about the imaging methodology.

claim: Participants performed an object-location memory task while freely navigating a 3D, virtual environment task adapted from Doeller et al.
source: Participants performed an object-location memory task while freely navigating a 3D, virtual environment task adapted from Doeller et al. (Doeller et al, 2008; Doeller et al., 2010) (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about the experimental task, with reference to Figure 5A and citations to Doeller et al., 2008 and Doeller et al., 2010.

claim: Participants were presented with pictures of spatial and non-spatial stimuli and gave a trial-by-trial animacy judgement.
source: Participants were presented with pictures of spatial and non-spatial stimuli (see Figure 5B) and gave a trial-by-trial animacy judgement.
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about the experimental task, with reference to Figure 5B.

claim: Data pre-processing included motion correction in SPM8, data de-noising with the FIX artifact removal procedure implemented in FSL 5.0.4, and nonlinear normalisation to a group-specific EPI template with the Advanced Neuroimaging Toolbox.
source: Pre-processing included motion correction in SPM8 (http://www.fil.ion.ucl.ac.uk/spm), data de-noising with the FIX artifact removal procedure implemented in FSL 5.0.4 (http://fsl.fmrib.ox.ac.uk/fsl/) that has been trained manually on 10 of the 22 participants and nonlinear normalisation to a group-specific EPI template with the Advanced Neuroimaging Toolbox (Avants et al., 2011) (ANTS; http://www.picsl.upenn.edu/ANTS/).
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about the data processing methodology.

claim: The functional data were smoothed with a full-width at half-maximum (FWHM) Gaussian kernel of 2.5 mm3.
source: The functional data were smoothed with a full-width at half-maximum (FWHM) Gaussian kernel of 2.5 mm3 (roughly 2.5 times the voxel size) to increase the SNR and improve ICA-based data de-noising with the FIX procedure (see above) while maintaining high spatial resolution for connectivity analyses.
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about the data processing methodology.

claim: An EC ROI was manually defined with ITK Snap 3.2 on the group-specific high-resolution mean EPI template from the navigation experiment.
source: For the 7 Tesla experiments (navigation experiment and spatial and non-spatial stimulation experiment), an EC ROI was manually defined with ITK Snap 3.2 (Yushkevich et al., 2006) (http://www.itksnap.org) on the group-specific high-resolution mean EPI template from the navigation experiment.
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about the ROI definition methodology.

claim: The posterior border of the EC was set to ∼1.5 mm posterior to the gyrus intralimbicus.
source: Based on anatomical landmarks as described by Insausti et al., (1998) and Frankó et al., (2014), the posterior border of the EC was set to ∼1.5 mm posterior to the gyrus intralimbicus, the anterior border to ∼1.5 mm posterior to the limen insulae, the lateral border to the midpoint of the medial bank of the collateral sulcus and the medial border to the hippocampal fissure at the level of the uncus.
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about the ROI definition methodology, based on anatomical landmarks from Insausti et al., 1998 and Frankó et al., 2014.

claim: Functional connectivity was estimated by means of partial correlation analysis between the time-series of groups of ROIs.
source: For the quantification of the model-based analyses of connectivity between the AT and PM networks and the manually segmented medial and lateral or anterior and posterior EC, singular-value decomposition (SVD) and subtraction of the mean was performed on the voxel-wise time-series within each ROI. Next, functional connectivity was estimated by means of partial correlation analysis between the time-series of groups of ROIs.
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about the connectivity analysis methodology.

claim: ConGrads allows for tracing the dominant modes of functional connectivity change within a pre-specified region of the brain in a fully data-driven manner.
source: To overcome limitations of the seed-based connectivity analysis, we employed ConGrads (Haak et al., 2014), which allows for tracing the dominant modes of functional connectivity change within a pre-specified region of the brain in a fully data-driven manner.
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about the ConGrads method, with citation to Haak et al., 2014.

claim: The LE algorithm maximizes topology preservation.
source: Because the LE algorithm maximizes topology preservation, we report the correlation coefficients without p-values.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the Laplacian Eigenmaps algorithm.

claim: Clustering was performed on the high-resolution data from the navigation experiment by grouping voxels above and below the median value of each mode of functional connectivity change.
source: Clustering was performed on the high-resolution data from the navigation experiment by grouping voxels above and below the median value of each mode of functional connectivity change, which resulted in two equally sized clusters per mode of connectivity change.
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about the clustering methodology.

claim: tSNR was determined by dividing the mean signal within a region by the standard deviation of that signal over time.
source: tSNR was determined by dividing the mean signal within a region by the standard deviation of that signal over time.
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about the SNR calculation methodology.

claim: Spatial SNR was determined by dividing the mean signal within a region by the standard deviation of the signal across voxels.
source: Conversely, spatial SNR was determined by dividing the mean signal within a region by the standard deviation of the signal across voxels.
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about the SNR calculation methodology.
